description: Hi! I'm a computer science student with a background in C, C++, C#, and Unix/Linux systems. I'm participating in this year's NASA Space Apps Challenge as a solo team, building a web application using NASA's open data. I enjoy data processing, backend development, and turning complex data into clear, usable visualizations. I'm happy to share ideas and learn from other participants during the event!
summary: Fire Calendar is a free website that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any place on Earth. NASA has two fire records: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). VIIRS has smaller pixels and finds about 4.5 times more hotspots, so the two records cannot be compared directly. I measured, for each region, how many VIIRS hotspots correspond to one MODIS hotspot in the years when both satellites were working (2013-2019), and used this ratio to convert the older MODIS data. The result is one monthly record from December 2000 until now. Users can search a country, state, city or coordinates and see a year-by-month calendar with the usual burning season, unusual months (at least 1.5 times the usual level), the biggest months on record and how the current month is going. A 3D globe shows a monthly time-lapse of fires across the whole planet. This helps fire managers, responders and scientists see when burning is normal for a place and when a month is unusual.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Fire Calendar lets anyone pick an area (a country, a state or province, a city, or a latitude/longitude) and see a month-by-month calendar of burning activity from December 2000 to today. Each cell shows how many active fire hotspots were detected that month, in VIIRS-equivalent units, and how this compares with the usual level for that calendar month. Users can switch to a "compared with usual" view, see unusual months (at least 1.5x their usual level), the biggest month on record, the current month's progress with a projection for the whole month, and download the calendar as CSV. A 3D globe with a monthly time-lapse shows where the planet is burning, and clicking anywhere opens that place's calendar.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: I downloaded all NASA FIRMS active fire hotspots from MODIS (Nov 2000 onward) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m (Jan 2012 onward), standard and near-real-time products, through the FIRMS API, and counted them per month on a 0.25 x 0.25 degree global grid.

2. Harmonization: VIIRS detects far more small fires than MODIS. For every region I compute ratio = VIIRS hotspots / MODIS hotspots over the 84 overlap months 2013-2019. If the region has too few fires (under 300 MODIS hotspots), the ratio comes from a 4-degree wider area, and otherwise from the whole world. Examples: California 4.41, world 4.55. Months with VIIRS data use VIIRS directly; earlier months use MODIS x ratio and are clearly marked as estimated.

3. Calendar statistics: "usual" is the median of the same calendar month across all years. Months with incomplete data are shown as missing, never as zero. Months that exist only in near-real-time data are marked provisional.

4. Regions: country and state boundaries come from Natural Earth (public domain); a region is the set of grid cells whose centre lies inside its boundary. Cities and coordinates use the 1 x 1 degree cell around the point.

5. Architecture: a Python pipeline (pandas, NumPy, shapely) pre-computes calendars for 4,854 regions and about 19,500 one-degree cells. The website is fully static (HTML/JavaScript, globe.gl), hosted for free on GitHub Pages, with no server and no external services at run time, so it is fast, cheap to keep online and easy to update.

VALIDATION

Known fire events stand out clearly: California's Thomas fire (Dec 2017), Camp fire (Nov 2018), the record 2020 season (Sep 2020, about 20x the usual September) and the Los Angeles fires (Jan 2025). The Sahel's dry-season burning belt appears in the right months. I checked that the static website gives the same results as the original server code, and that the browser code reproduces the Python statistics exactly.

LIMITATIONS

Estimated (MODIS-only) months are approximate (roughly +-20-30% per month). Hotspot counts measure detected burning activity, not burned area or intensity; clouds and smoke hide some fires. Unusual months with very few hotspots are mostly noise.

FUTURE

Ratios per season, adding the NOAA-20/21 VIIRS satellites, burned-area products, and email alerts when a region's current month is running well above its usual level.

Source code and full method: https://github.com/derinceyhan25/nasa-space-apps-2026

Tools: Python, pandas, NumPy, shapely, JavaScript, globe.gl / three.js, GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions.
